It contains a single superfamily, c.2.1, whose families include the alcohol dehydrogenase-like NAD-binding domain (c.2.1.1), tyrosine-dependent oxidoreductases / short-chain dehydrogenase-reductases (c.2.1.2), GAPDH-like N-terminal domains (c.2.1.3), formate/glycerate dehydrogenase NAD domains (c.2.1.4), lactate/malate dehydrogenase N-terminal domains (c.2.1.5), 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase-like N-terminal domains (c.2.1.6), amino-acid dehydrogenase-like C-terminal domains (c.2.1.7), CoA-binding domains (c.2.1.8) and the TrkA-type potassium-channel NAD-binding domain (c.2.1.9).
- c.3 FAD/NAD(P)-binding domain (superfamily c.3.1): a different fold (central 5-stranded sheet 32145 plus an antiparallel 3-stranded meander) used by glutathione reductase, p-hydroxybenzoate hydroxylase and related flavoenzymes.
- c.4 Nucleotide-binding domain (c.4.1): a 5-stranded 32145 Rossmann-like sheet found in, for example, dihydrodipicolinate reductase and UDP-glucose dehydrogenase N-terminal domains.
- c.5 MurCD N-terminal domain; c.31 DHS-like NAD/FAD-binding domain (c.31.1), which includes the NAD-dependent sirtuin deacetylases, the deoxyhypusine synthase and the TPP-enzyme pyr domain; c.66 S-adenosyl-L-methionine-dependent methyltransferases, a Rossmann-like but separately classified fold.
- Non-Rossmann solutions: c.1.7 NAD(P)-linked oxidoreductase (aldo-keto reductases) binds NADPH in an extended conformation at the C-terminal end of a TIM (b/a)8 barrel; c.82 ALDDH-like (aldehyde dehydrogenase) binds NAD(P) to a Rossmann-like 5-stranded domain without the canonical GxGxxG motif; c.71 Dihydrofolate reductase-like binds NADPH on a distinct a/b fold; c.23 flavodoxin-like proteins bind FMN/NAD(P)H; d.166 ADP-ribosylation enzymes (toxins, PARPs) and c.26.2 adenine-nucleotide alpha hydrolase-like enzymes (NAD synthetase) use NAD as a substrate on yet other folds; the catalytic domain of medium-chain alcohol dehydrogenases is an all-beta GroES-like domain (b.35) separate from its c.2.1.1 Rossmann domain.

What this implies about convergence versus divergence, by hierarchy level:
- Class (c, alpha/beta): says nothing about ancestry; it only groups secondary-structure composition.
- Fold: shared topology only. SCOP explicitly states that fold membership does not imply homology. The SCOP curators even annotate that the nucleotide-binding modes of c.2, c.3 and c.4 are similar, yet they keep them as separate folds. That is the clearest statement in the database that similar cofactor binding was judged insufficient to merge them into one superfamily. The three-layer a/b/a sandwich with a central parallel sheet is a 'superfold': it is a physically favoured architecture, and the NAD(P) pyrophosphate binding at the N-terminus of the first helix (the helix-dipole and glycine-rich GxGxxG/GxGxxA turn) is a low-complexity chemical solution that can be, and apparently has been, reinvented. Aldo-keto reductases (c.1.7) and dihydrofolate reductase (c.71) show that even the general Rossmann architecture is not necessary: NAD(P)H can be bound productively by completely different folds. So across folds the picture is convergent evolution of function, or at least no detectable common ancestry.
- Superfamily: this is the level at which SCOP asserts probable common ancestry. Within c.2.1 the lactate, malate, alcohol, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, 6-phosphogluconate and short-chain dehydrogenases share the sheet order, the GxGxxG fingerprint in the beta1-alphaA turn, the acidic residue at the C-terminus of beta2 that hydrogen-bonds the adenosine 2'-OH (replaced by basic residues in NADP-specific members), and the same adenine-binding sub-site, with family-level sequence similarity bridging many of them. That combination of structural, positional and sequence evidence, not the cofactor itself, is what justifies divergent evolution from one ancestral nucleotide-binding domain. Note that c.2.1 also contains CoA-binding domains and non-catalytic regulatory domains (TrkA, the NAD-binding domains of some transcription regulators), so the superfamily is defined by ancestry, not by NAD(P) binding.
- Family: clear sequence similarity (typically >30% identity or very strong profile matches) and usually conserved function; this is the only level at which function and mechanism can be transferred with confidence.

Why cofactor binding or active-site similarity alone is not evidence of homology:
1. Functional convergence is common because chemistry constrains the solution space. NAD(P) is one molecule, hydride transfer requires the nicotinamide C4 to be positioned next to a substrate, and the pyrophosphate wants a positively polarized helix N-terminus. Many independent sequences can satisfy that, so similarity in the cofactor site is expected even without common descent. Similar reasoning applies to catalytic triads, metal sites and phosphate-binding P-loops.
2. Active-site residues are under the strongest selection and are the least informative about descent: convergent sites (serine proteases of folds b.47 and c.41; carbonic anhydrases; aldolase classes) are textbook cases where identical catalytic geometry arose on unrelated scaffolds.
3. Conversely, within a true superfamily cofactor specificity and even catalysis are not conserved: NAD versus NADP preference can switch with one or two residues at the end of beta2, and c.2.1 holds members that bind CoA or nothing. If the cofactor is not conserved among homologs and is shared among non-homologs, it cannot by itself diagnose homology.
4. Short motifs such as GxGxxG are statistically weak; a 6-residue glycine-rich turn recurs by chance and by convergence, and it is also present in the c.3 FAD-binding fold that SCOP keeps separate.

Evidence SCOP-style curation actually requires for a homology (superfamily) call, and what one should look for before transferring function: statistically significant sequence or profile-profile similarity (PSI-BLAST, HMM-HMM) that aligns the conserved motifs onto structurally equivalent positions; shared unusual structural features beyond the common core (same topology plus the same idiosyncratic insertions, crossover connections or strand order); conservation of functional residues at equivalent positions in the alignment; intermediate sequences linking families; and, where possible, consistent gene context or domain-combination evidence. Structural similarity, cofactor identity and catalytic chemistry are each necessary-but-not-sufficient, and SCOP only declares a superfamily when several lines converge.

Practical limits that follow: (a) a SCOPe fold-level match between a query and an NAD(P)-binding domain does not justify annotating the query as an NAD(P) enzyme, and a c.2.1 superfamily match does not justify assigning substrate or NAD/NADP specificity, which must come from family-level similarity or experiment; (b) the choice of template for homology modelling of a cofactor site should be within the same family, or at minimum the same superfamily with an alignment that preserves the GxGxxG turn and the beta2 specificity residue, never a merely fold-level analog; (c) the SCOP fold boundaries among c.2, c.3, c.4, c.5, c.31 and c.66 are conservative hypotheses, and some authors argue for deep common ancestry among Rossmann-like folds, so 'different fold' in SCOPe should be read as 'no accepted evidence of homology' rather than proven independent origin; (d) ASTRAL representative sets chosen by sequence identity thresholds will include many c.2.1 domains with similar cofactor sites, so representative selection should be at the superfamily or family level rather than by ligand.

prompt: How did the relationship between the ColG collagenase domain in PDB 1nqd and the Cry3A C-terminal domain in PDB 1dlc change from SCOPe 2.04 to current SCOPe, and what structural and functional evidence supports their common ancestry?
answer:
Short answer: the premise of a reclassification is not supported. I am aware of no SCOPe change between release 2.04 and the current 2.0x releases that moved the ColG domain in 1nqd and the Cry3A C-terminal domain in 1dlc into a shared superfamily, or that otherwise altered the stated evolutionary relationship between them. Both entries predate 2.04 by a decade, their hierarchy placements were set during the manually curated SCOP 1.x era that SCOPe inherited, and post-2.04 SCOPe releases (2.05 through 2.08 and later) added mostly automated classifications of newer PDB entries plus incremental curation. Pre-existing placements of old entries were rarely revised, and I have no recollection of a curator note, merge, or split touching either of these domains. Treat any claim of a 2.04-to-current change as unverified until checked against the release-specific dir.cla/dir.des files and the SCOPe change logs.

Two corrections to the named entities, because they change the answer.

First, 1nqd is not the collagenase catalytic domain. It is the C-terminal collagen-binding domain (CBD, the s3b segment) of ColG from Hathewaya (Clostridium) histolytica, roughly 120 residues, solved by Wilson, Matsushita, Okabe and Sakon (EMBO J 2003) and described as a beta-sheet sandwich carrying a novel calcium-binding motif that rigidifies the domain and sets its orientation relative to the neighbouring PKD-like domain. The ColG zinc peptidase (catalytic) domain is a gluzincin-type M9B metallopeptidase and was only solved much later, in separate entries from around 2011 to 2012. If the question intends the catalytic domain, the answer is trivially negative: a thermolysin-like alpha/beta zinc peptidase and an all-beta lectin-like sandwich share no fold, no superfamily, and no plausible common ancestry.

Second, 1dlc is the three-domain Cry3A delta-endotoxin of Bacillus thuringiensis subsp. tenebrionis (Li, Carroll and Ellar, Nature 1991). SCOP/SCOPe splits it into three separate domains: an N-terminal alpha-helical bundle, a middle beta-prism-like domain, and the C-terminal domain, which is the all-beta jelly-roll sandwich at issue here. My recollection is that the C-terminal domain sits in SCOPe class b with the galactose-binding-domain-like / lectin-like beta-sandwich region of the hierarchy, as its own delta-endotoxin C-terminal domain family. I do not trust my recall of the exact sccs string or sunid, so I am deliberately not quoting one.

What the structural evidence actually supports. Both domains are small all-beta sandwiches of the lectin-like / carbohydrate-binding-module flavour, both bind calcium, and both serve as accessory targeting modules appended to a catalytic or pore-forming effector. That is a real and reproducible similarity at the fold and architecture level, and structure-comparison servers will return respectable superpositions over the sandwich core. But beta-sandwich jelly rolls are among the most convergently reinvented folds in the PDB. Shared sandwich topology plus a calcium site is weak evidence for divergence from a common ancestor, because calcium sites recur independently in loop-rich beta-sandwiches, and because the two domains differ in strand count, loop decoration, and the location and coordination chemistry of their metal sites. SCOP-style classification would require placing them in one superfamily only if there were evidence of common ancestry beyond topology, and the published record I am aware of does not meet that bar. The defensible statement is fold-level or analogy-level similarity, not superfamily-level homology.

Functional evidence argues against, not for, transfer. The ColG CBD binds the collagen triple helix and tethers the protease to insoluble fibrillar substrate; its binding surface and calcium loop are collagen-specific and the domain has no catalytic activity of its own. The Cry3A C-terminal domain functions in the insect midgut context as a receptor-interaction and structural-stability module in a pore-forming toxin, with reported sugar-binding character and a role in holding the toxin fold together. There is no shared ligand, no shared binding site, and no shared catalytic chemistry. Unsafe transfers to avoid: do not infer collagen binding for the Cry3A domain, do not infer membrane or receptor interaction for the ColG CBD, do not carry the ColG calcium-binding motif annotation across as a conserved family feature, and do not use 1dlc as a comparative-modelling template for 1nqd or the reverse. At this level of similarity a template would misplace loops and the metal site even where the sandwich core superposes acceptably. Note also that each PDB entry here contributes only one representative conformation; ASTRAL representative selection at 40 or 95 percent identity picks one domain per cluster and says nothing about evolutionary relatedness between clusters.

External evidence that would be required to upgrade this to common ancestry: a structure-based alignment with a significant and length-corrected score (DALI Z well above background for a sandwich of this size, plus TM-align with manual inspection of strand correspondence, not score alone); profile-to-profile or HMM-to-HMM detection linking the two sequence families (HHpred or a shared Pfam clan assignment); a conserved sequence or structural motif beyond topology, ideally functional residues in equivalent positions; agreement from an independent hierarchy, since ECOD explicitly separates possible-homology X-groups from asserted-homology H-groups and its verdict on these two domains is the cleanest cross-check; and taxonomic or genomic-context evidence such as intermediate homologues bridging the two families. Absent at least profile-level linkage plus motif conservation, the correct classification language is analogous fold, and the correct answer to the question as posed is that the relationship did not change.

prompt: d1p7jd_ and d1ztra1 share homeodomain family a.4.1.1, but d1ztra1 has an hf annotation. What remains justified about homology, and why should the structures not be treated as interchangeable templates or training examples?
answer:
What stays justified: both domains sit in SCOPe family a.4.1.1 (Homeodomain), inside superfamily a.4.1 (Homeodomain-like) and fold a.4 (DNA/RNA-binding 3-helical bundle), class a (all-alpha). Family-level placement in SCOP/SCOPe is the strongest evolutionary claim: it asserts clear, usually sequence-detectable homology, so d1p7jd_ and d1ztra1 are confidently inferred to descend from a common homeodomain ancestor, to share the canonical three-helix bundle with helix 3 as the DNA-recognition helix, and to share the conserved hydrophobic core positions (e.g. the W48/F49 region) that define the homeodomain signature. That homology inference does not depend on either structure being a perfect representative; the hf flag does not demote the pair to superfamily-only (a.4.1, homology inferred from structure/function but weaker sequence signal) or fold-only (a.4, which contains non-homologous 3-helical bundles such as some winged-helix relatives placed in other superfamilies and must never be read as common ancestry).

What the hf annotation changes: in SCOPe a domain carrying this annotation is flagged as a heterogeneous/irregular member of its family rather than a clean canonical instance. In practice this means the deposited region used for d1ztra1 (note the 'a1' suffix: a defined region of chain A, not the whole chain, so the chain was split or contains additional material) does not map onto the family in the simple one-chain-one-domain way that d1p7jd_ does (the '_' suffix means the whole chain D was classified as the domain). Typical reasons for such flags in this family are: the domain is a fragment or an extended construct with extra N-/C-terminal helices or linker (as in POU-homeodomain, paired-class, TALE/PBX-class homeodomains with their three-residue insertion between helices 1 and 2, or HNF1-type atypical homeodomains); it is part of a fusion or multi-domain chain; it is an NMR ensemble or low-resolution/partially disordered model; or it was placed by automated matching to an existing family entry rather than by manual curation. Any of these make the structural coverage, helix lengths, loop conformations and DNA-contact geometry of d1ztra1 non-representative of a.4.1.1 as a whole.

Why they are not interchangeable templates: (1) Template suitability is a structural-similarity and completeness question, not a homology question. A family label guarantees a shared core of roughly 50-60 residues, but the hf member may lack or add elements, so using it as a template would propagate missing residues, construct-specific helix extensions or artefactual loop geometry into a model; equally, using the canonical d1p7jd_ for a target that actually resembles the atypical member would mis-model the insertion/extension. Choose the template by sequence identity to the target, alignment coverage and resolution/experimental quality, and verify core RMSD and the recognition-helix register, rather than by family identity alone. (2) Function transfer is also not safe by family label: homeodomains with different residue 50 (Q50, K50, S50 classes) and different N-terminal arms recognise different DNA sites, and some family members act as heterodimers (e.g. MATa1/MATalpha2, Hox/Pbx), so DNA specificity, partner binding and the biological role of d1p7jd_ must not be assumed for d1ztra1 or vice versa without experimental binding or genetic evidence. (3) As training examples, the two domains are not equivalent samples of the family: including the hf domain as a 'clean' a.4.1.1 positive would inject boundary and coverage noise into fold/family classifiers, and including both as independent examples in a split can leak near-duplicate information. Representative selection (e.g. SCOPe Astral subsets at 40% or 95% identity, or a hand-picked canonical structure) should prefer the whole-chain, manually curated, high-quality member and should explicitly exclude or down-weight hf-flagged domains, or at least carry the flag as metadata.

Required external evidence before treating them as equivalent: the actual SCOPe domain boundary definitions and the 2.0x release in which the hf flag was assigned, the PDB entry headers (method, resolution, construct, presence of DNA or partner chains), a pairwise structural superposition over the shared core, and sequence identity between the two domains. Without those, the only safe statement is that the two domains are homologous homeodomains, not that they are structurally or functionally substitutable. prompt: d1uc6a1 and d1o5dt2 belong to fibronectin type III family b.1.2.1, but d1o5dt2 is annotated as a fragment. How should that annotation affect alignment, representative selection, and interpretation of family diversity?
answer:
Both d1uc6a1 and d1o5dt2 are classified in SCOPe family b.1.2.1 (fibronectin type III), superfamily b.1.2 (fibronectin type III), fold b.1 (immunoglobulin-like beta-sandwich), class b (all-beta). The family assignment is the strongest statement SCOPe makes: it asserts clear homology between the two domains, so the fragment annotation does not weaken the evolutionary claim. What the fragment annotation changes is how much of the FN3 fold is actually present in d1o5dt2 and therefore how the entry should be used.

Meaning of the annotation. In SCOPe a 'fragment' label on a domain (carried in the domain/protein description and visible in the dir.des/dir.cla files and on the domain page) indicates that the classified region covers only part of a canonical domain: the construct was truncated, or part of the domain was disordered/unobserved in the deposited coordinates, so one or more of the seven FN3 beta-strands (A, B, C, C', E, F, G) of the roughly 90-100 residue beta-sandwich are missing or incomplete. The classification was made because the observed portion is still recognizably FN3 and homologous to the family, not because the fragment is a complete, independently folded unit. (I am answering from model knowledge only and have not re-checked the 1O5D or 1UC6 PDB records, so I cannot state exactly which strands are absent; that should be confirmed from the SCOPe domain boundaries and the PDB SEQRES/observed-residue comparison.)

Effect on alignment. (1) Align the fragment to a complete FN3 domain such as d1uc6a1 rather than the reverse; the complete domain defines the frame, and residues absent in d1o5dt2 should be treated as missing data (not as deletions, loop shortenings, or strand loss). (2) Use ASTRAL's distinction between observed-residue (os) and genetic-domain (gd) sequences: the gd sequence derived from SEQRES may show residues that are present in the construct but unobserved, while the os sequence shows only modeled residues; the fragment annotation often means even the SEQRES region is truncated. (3) Sequence identity or structural similarity computed over a short overlap is unreliable: a fragment can give inflated identity (short, conserved core only) or deflated scores (missing half of the sandwich lowers TM-score/DALI Z), so coverage must be reported alongside identity, and structure superposition should be restricted to the shared strands rather than forced over the whole domain. (4) Do not use the fragment to infer the position of FN3 loops (BC, C'E, FG) that are not in the structure; those loops are the regions most often engineered or functionally variable, and absent data is not evidence of absence.

Effect on representative selection. SCOPe/ASTRAL subsets (e.g., the 40% and 95% identity non-redundant sets) are built by clustering and then picking the domain with the best SPACI/AEROSPACI quality score (resolution, R-factors, stereochemistry) within each cluster; fragments are not automatically excluded, and NMR entries receive no resolution-based score, so a fragment can still be selected if its cluster has no better complete member. For any downstream use (homology modeling template, fold-recognition benchmark, structural alignment seed, family profile/HMM seed) a fragment should be deprioritized: prefer a complete, high-quality domain such as d1uc6a1 (or another full-length b.1.2.1 domain with better SPACI) as the family representative, and keep d1o5dt2 only as an additional member whose covered region is noted. If d1o5dt2 is the sole representative of a sequence cluster, the cluster is under-described and the gap in coverage should be flagged rather than silently filled by the fragment. The fragment is also unsuitable as a template for modeling a full FN3 domain because missing strands would have to be modeled from another template, and its coordinates should not be used to define domain boundaries for new genomic FN3 domains.

Effect on interpreting family diversity. The b.1.2.1 family already contains many FN3 domains from diverse proteins (fibronectin, tenascin, cytokine receptors, kinases, adhesion molecules), with low pairwise sequence identity but a conserved fold. A fragment inflates apparent diversity if its shortness is misread as a distinct, minimal FN3 architecture, and it can distort clustering because its short overlap places it into a cluster artefactually. It should therefore not be counted as evidence of a new subfamily, a novel strand topology, or unusual domain length; variation in loop lengths and strand register across the family should be measured only on complete domains. Conversely, the fragment's membership in b.1.2.1 still legitimately documents that the parent protein contains an FN3 domain, which is useful for domain-architecture surveys as long as the length is not taken at face value.

Limits on homology and function transfer. Family membership supports homology between d1uc6a1 and d1o5dt2 but does not imply shared molecular function: FN3 domains are generic beta-sandwich modules whose binding partners differ widely (integrin-binding RGD in fibronectin FN3-10, cytokine binding in receptor FN3 domains, structural spacer roles elsewhere), so no ligand or functional site should be transferred between these two domains without independent experimental or sequence-motif evidence. Relationships above the family level are weaker still: other b.1.2 superfamily members share probable common ancestry, while fold-level neighbors such as immunoglobulin domains (b.1.1) or other b.1 superfamilies share only the beta-sandwich topology and must not be assumed homologous. For the fragment specifically, functional inference is doubly limited because the surface that might carry a binding site may be the very part that is missing, and the observed conformation of the partial sandwich may be perturbed by loss of its packing partner strands (fragment structures often come from complexes, where the fragment's conformation is stabilized by a partner chain). Any claim about the fragment's binding mode or stability therefore needs external evidence such as the full-length structure of the same protein, biochemical binding data, or a sequence alignment of the complete parental domain to the family profile.

prompt: A newly solved domain resembles a known SCOPe fold but lacks convincing evidence of common ancestry with any existing superfamily. Should it be assigned to a new family, a new superfamily in the existing fold, or a new fold? What biological claim does each choice make?
answer:
Recommended assignment: a new superfamily within the existing fold (not a new family inside an existing superfamily, and not a new fold). Reasoning by SCOPe level, each of which encodes a distinct evolutionary claim:

1. New family within an existing superfamily. In SCOPe, families group domains with clear evidence of common ancestry: typically >=30% pairwise sequence identity, or lower identity backed by very similar structure plus shared function (e.g., conserved catalytic residues, shared ligands). Placing the new domain in a new family inside an existing superfamily asserts 'this is a homolog of the other families in that superfamily, merely a more distant one.' Because the new domain lacks convincing evidence of common ancestry with any superfamily, this choice overstates the evidence. It would also license unsafe transfer: superfamily-level annotation (functional mechanism, active-site location, ligand binding) would be inherited by implication, and the domain could be used as a template for homology-based inference that is not justified.

2. New superfamily within the existing fold. SCOPe superfamilies contain families whose members are inferred to share a probable common evolutionary origin despite low sequence identity, based on structural and functional features (unusual shared structural motifs, common functional sites, conserved rare features). Distinct superfamilies within one fold are, by definition, NOT asserted to be homologous: the fold level is a statement about major secondary-structure composition, arrangement, and topological connections, which SCOP/SCOPe explicitly treat as potentially arising by convergence (physics/chemistry favoring certain folds, e.g., Rossmann-like, TIM barrels, ferredoxin-like). So a new superfamily in the existing fold makes exactly the biological claim the evidence supports: 'this domain has the same core architecture and topology as these other domains, but we do not claim it is descended from a common ancestor with any of them.' This is the SCOP convention for the described situation, and it is how the many-superfamily folds (e.g., TIM beta/alpha-barrel c.1, ferredoxin-like d.58, four-helical up-and-down bundle f.1 / a.24) were built up.

3. New fold. A new fold asserts that the core secondary-structure elements, their spatial arrangement, or their topological connectivity differ substantially from any existing fold. Since the question states the domain resembles a known fold, creating a new fold would be a false negative at the architecture level: it would claim a structural novelty that does not exist and would fragment structure-similarity searches. New folds are reserved for genuinely new topologies, not for cases where only the ancestry inference is uncertain. (SCOPe does allow 'multidomain' or 'small protein' exceptions and some fold definitions are themselves hypotheses, but that does not apply here.)

Key principles and limits:
- The SCOPe hierarchy is an explicit set of nested evolutionary hypotheses: family = clear homology; superfamily = probable but distant homology; fold = structural similarity that may be convergent; class = secondary-structure content only. Assigning at the lowest level supported by evidence (and no lower) is the conservative, correct practice.
- The new superfamily is a provisional hypothesis. It should be revised (merged into an existing superfamily, as SCOP historically did) if later evidence appears: intermediate sequences linking the two via profile/HMM searches, shared unusual structural features (e.g., a rare beta-bulge, cis-peptide, or circular permutation shared only by the two groups), conserved functional-site geometry with equivalent catalytic residues, shared cofactor or ligand binding at the same location, or genomic/operon context. Conversely, if the newly solved domain has sufficient sequence identity to an existing family it must go there, regardless of surface structural impressions.
- Function transfer: from a superfamily-level or fold-level neighbor, function must not be transferred by default. Fold-mates are frequently functionally unrelated (TIM barrels, Rossmann-like folds). Even within a superfamily, function can diverge. Only family-level membership (and often not even that) justifies annotating function by inheritance; specific residues must still be checked.
- Template/representative use: the structural neighbors in the fold can serve as geometric templates for fold recognition or threading, but not for homology modeling with evolutionary claims (e.g., alignments of conserved positions, active-site mapping). The new domain would become the first and sole representative of its superfamily/family; SCOPe representative selection (e.g., ASTRAL 40% or 95% identity subsets) would include it as a singleton, so any benchmark counting superfamily-level homologs would correctly treat it as having none.
- Release-specific caveat: SCOPe (2.01 through 2.08) adds new entries mostly by automated classification of structures with clear sequence similarity to existing entries; genuinely new superfamilies and folds require manual curation and were added sparingly. A domain of the described kind would be a manually curated addition rather than an automated one, and its classification remains an expert judgment rather than a measurable fact.

prompt: Canonical protein kinases, aminoglycoside phosphotransferases, and phosphoinositide 3-kinases have related catalytic-domain architecture in SCOPe. What common evolutionary or mechanistic conclusions are justified, and what evidence is needed before transferring substrate specificity or regulation?
answer:
SCOPe placement. All three groups sit in class d (alpha+beta), fold d.144 'Protein kinase-like (PK-like)', superfamily d.144.1 'Protein kinase-like (PK-like)', but in different families: d.144.1.1 Phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) catalytic domain (e.g. PI3Kgamma, PDB 1E8X), d.144.1.2 Aminoglycoside phosphotransferases (e.g. APH(3')-IIIa, PDB 1J7L/1L8T), and d.144.1.7 Protein kinases, catalytic subunit (e.g. PKA, d1atpe_ from 1ATP; the canonical eukaryotic protein kinase family that also contains Ser/Thr and Tyr kinases). Other members of the same superfamily include choline kinase (d.144.1.4), actin-fragmin kinase (d.144.1.3) and the lipid/PI4K-related families; the fold's defining feature is a bilobal catalytic core with a mostly beta N-lobe and mostly alpha C-lobe, ATP bound in the cleft between them. These fold/superfamily/family assignments are stable across the SCOPe 2.0x releases (2.01 through 2.08) because new structures are added to existing families by automated classification rather than by re-drawing superfamily boundaries.

What is justified. (1) Homology: shared superfamily membership in SCOP/SCOPe is a curated claim of probable common ancestry, supported here by conserved motifs beyond mere shape: the beta3 lysine that positions the ATP alpha/beta phosphates, the catalytic-loop aspartate (HRD in ePKs; the Brenner motif HGDxxxxN in APHs; an equivalent Asp in PI3Ks), and the Mg-binding aspartate (DFG in ePKs; the DxD/ID segment of APHs; DRH/DFG-like in PI3Ks). (2) Mechanism: all catalyse direct, Mg2+-dependent in-line transfer of the ATP gamma-phosphate to a hydroxyl acceptor with no phosphoenzyme intermediate; the bilobal closure around ATP and the role of the catalytic Asp/Mg pair are transferable mechanistic conclusions. (3) ATP-site similarity: it is legitimate to expect cross-reactivity of ATP-competitive inhibitors (ePK inhibitors inhibit APHs; wortmannin/LY294002 hit PI3Ks and PI3K-related kinases; some ePK inhibitors hit PI3Ks), which is an inference about the nucleotide pocket, not about substrates.

What is NOT justified at superfamily level. Substrate specificity and regulation are family- or subfamily-level properties and do not follow from d.144.1 membership. ePKs phosphorylate Ser/Thr/Tyr on protein substrates presented by the activation segment and P+1 loop; APHs phosphorylate hydroxyls of aminoglycoside antibiotics (small molecules bound in an acidic C-lobe pocket) and mostly lack a protein-substrate groove, even though a few APHs show weak Ser kinase activity; PI3Ks phosphorylate the 3-OH of inositol lipid headgroups, with class I/II/III specificity set by activation-loop basic residues, and the PI3K-related kinases (mTOR, ATM, DNA-PK) in the same family are protein kinases, so even within d.144.1.1 substrate type varies. Regulation is likewise non-transferable: ePKs use activation-loop phosphorylation, alphaC-helix/regulatory-spine assembly and the glycine-rich loop (a motif APHs and PI3Ks largely lack); APHs are essentially constitutive; PI3Ks are controlled by regulatory subunits (p85 SH2/iSH2), Ras binding via the RBD, and membrane recruitment through C2/helical domains. Transferring 'activation loop' logic to an APH, or p85-type regulation to a protein kinase, would be an unsafe transfer. Equally unsafe: assuming a sequence that merely matches the PK-like fold is catalytically active (pseudokinases keep the fold but lose the Lys/HRD/DFG residues), or using PKA as a template to model the substrate site of an APH or PI3K; template selection should be at family level and guided by sequence identity in the substrate-binding segments, not by shared superfamily.

Evidence required before transferring specificity or regulation. (a) Phylogenetic/sequence evidence placing the query within a specific family or subfamily (e.g. HMM or profile hits with high identity across the whole catalytic domain, not just the ATP motifs). (b) Conservation of the actual substrate-recognition residues: activation segment and P+1 loop (ePK Ser/Thr vs Tyr determinants), the acidic aminoglycoside pocket and C-terminal subdomain of APHs, the activation-loop basic residues of PI3Ks. (c) Presence of the characteristic regulatory motifs/domains: glycine-rich loop, phosphorylatable activation-loop residue, alphaC-helix glutamate and regulatory spine for ePKs; RBD, C2, helical and p85-binding regions for PI3Ks; absence of these in APH-like proteins. (d) Direct biochemical data: enzyme kinetics and substrate profiling with protein, aminoglycoside and lipid substrates, mutagenesis of catalytic and specificity residues, and dependence on candidate regulators (phosphorylation, regulatory subunits, membranes, Ras). (e) Structural evidence of substrate or product complexes (or at least peptide/aminoglycoside/lipid-analog complexes) for the query or a close family member, rather than apo or nucleotide-only structures. (f) Genetic or physiological evidence (resistance phenotype for APH, signalling output for ePK/PI3K). Without such data, the only safe statements are shared ancestry, a shared bilobal PK-like fold, a shared Mg/Asp-dependent phosphoryl-transfer mechanism, and likely inhibitor cross-reactivity at the ATP site.
